# Pattern Decoder: full text

> 335 tactics and their patterns, in plain words. A reading aid, not a diagnosis. Licence: CC BY-NC-ND 4.0, by Shae Stovell, Noble Father Creations.

## Smear Campaigns

URL: https://noblefathercreations.com/playbook/smear-campaigns
Also called: Reputation Poisoning, Reputation Warfare (Post-Separation), Smear Campaign, Reputation Warfare, Smear Campaign (Preemptive), Smear Campaign (Reactive), Untraceable Seeding

Someone spreads a distorted story about you to the people whose view of you matters. You end up doubted or dropped, and your own account is heard as a reaction.

Safety: A smear alone is not physical danger. It becomes a safety matter when it comes with tracking, repeated filings or threats. It also does if there is a push to turn a court, employer or school against you. Do not answer the story in public or by contacting the person directly. Keep dated copies of what you can. Take them to legal aid or a domestic violence advocate who can advise on safe responses.

Signs it might be this:
- The same unusual detail or phrase shows up in different people's mouths, each saying they heard it from someone.
- The claims can be checked and are false or twisted, and correction changes nothing.
- Doubt about you was placed in someone's mind well before any conflict between you.
- The story follows you into new settings, such as a new job, club or relationship, soon after you join.
- Everyone has heard it and no one will say from whom.

Signs it is probably something else:
- Different people raise different concerns, each from their own contact with you.
- The people who doubt you can describe something they saw first-hand, and it is accurate.
- The claims are true, even if unflattering.
- Only one friend ever heard it, and it went no further.
- The cooling off matches ordinary distance after a split, and nobody repeats a story.
- What circulates is limited, accurate and fades as the dispute cools.
- The people who heard it are willing to hear your side, and some tell you what they were told.
- The talk ends within weeks and does not travel to new settings.

## Flying Monkeys / Proxy Recruitment

URL: https://noblefathercreations.com/playbook/flying-monkeys-proxy-recruitment
Also called: Proxy Recruitment, Flying Monkeys, Parental Amplification, Peer Pressure Weaponization, Proxy Control

People close to you start passing on someone else's demands or questions. They usually think they are helping, while the person behind it stays hidden.

Safety: Most messengers mean well, so this is not usually dangerous in itself. It becomes a safety matter when the questions are about where you live, who you are with or when you are alone. It also becomes one when contact keeps arriving after you have gone quiet to stay safe. Share nothing about your location or routine with anyone who might pass it on. Ask a domestic abuse advocate to help plan who can know what.

Signs it might be this:
- The messenger quotes details that only one person could have supplied, or uses that person's phrases.
- They tell you they were asked to get in touch, or let it slip.
- Several people with little recent contact raise the same issue within days.
- Their questions concern where you are, who you are with or what you plan to do, more than how you feel.
- What you say in reply reaches the original person, who then responds to your exact words.

Signs it is probably something else:
- The person has a record of reaching out on their own, with no sign of contact with the other side.
- They are as willing to hear your account as the other person's, and are clear they will not carry it back.
- Their concerns include things the other person never raised.
- Their worry looks the same whether or not you answer.
- They tell you plainly whose message it is and accept a no without pressing.
- The messenger is open about who asked them and accepts your answer without pressing.
- The contact happens once and ends when you reply.

## Triangulation

URL: https://noblefathercreations.com/playbook/triangulation
Also called: Central Positioning, Jealousy Manufacturing, Mirror Operation, Triangulation (Positive), Triangulation (Weaponized)

Instead of saying what they think, someone keeps telling you that other people agree with them. A two-person problem starts to feel like you against a group.

Signs it might be this:
- Other people's views are announced to you as a verdict rather than offered as one perspective.
- The quoted third person, when you ask them, says they never said it or were told something different.
- The speaker avoids saying what they personally want and keeps pointing to what others think.
- You learn a mutual friend or relative has been given a one-sided account before you were told there was a problem.
- Two people who used to get along start distrusting each other after both talked to the same go-between.

Signs it is probably something else:
- They name the person, say what was actually said, and invite you to ask that person yourself.
- The third person raised the concern on their own, and the speaker is passing it along because it matters.
- They state their own view first and mention another's only as a side note.
- The other people involved are openly present and speaking for themselves.
- It was a single mention during a heated moment and was not repeated or used again.
- The speaker is happy for you to speak with the people they mention.
- Other people's views come up rarely and as context, not as proof you must accept.
- When it turns out a quote was wrong, they correct it and drop the point.

## Group Consolidation

URL: https://noblefathercreations.com/playbook/group-consolidation

One person is punished in front of everyone, and the punishment is bigger than what they did. The rest of the group learns to keep their heads down.

Signs it might be this:
- The size of the penalty is clearly larger than the act that led to it.
- It was staged where others would see it, when a private conversation was available.
- The person punished had challenged a leader or a norm, and not broken a clear rule.
- Others in the group became visibly quieter and more cautious after it happened.
- People who made similar mistakes without challenging anyone were not treated the same way.

Signs it is probably something else:
- The same consequence has been applied in the same way to others, regardless of who watched.
- The person broke a clear, known rule, and the consequence matches what was written down.
- A private attempt to resolve it came first, and the visible step followed only after it failed.
- The response was about safety or the protection of others and not about dissent.
- Group members still raise concerns freely afterward and nothing changes in the room.
- The consequence is proportionate and follows a written or well-understood rule.
- The same response would have been given to anyone, whoever was watching.
- People feel free to ask about it afterward and receive honest answers.

## Silent Coalitions

URL: https://noblefathercreations.com/playbook/silent-coalitions
Also called: Ambient Exclusion, Silent Coalition Building

A group keeps one person on the edge through lots of small, hard-to-prove moments. The person starts to think the problem must be them.

Signs it might be this:
- Others who joined at the same time are included, and you are consistently not.
- The distance shows up across different settings, such as work, chat and social events.
- One-on-one, people are warm, but in the group the warmth disappears.
- A trusted outside person has seen the pattern on their own.
- When you name it, the group responds with matching denials and no curiosity about how it feels to you.

Signs it is probably something else:
- The feeling comes and goes with your mood and fades when you are rested or in better spirits.
- You can find examples of the group including you in the last month.
- Another person in the group feels equally left out, which suggests a loose group and not a target.
- When you ask directly, someone explains a reason and the exclusion stops.
- Your own contact has dropped, so replies simply mirror yours.
- Comparing notes shows that others feel the same way and the group is simply loose.
- Asking directly leads to an explanation and a change.

## Ostracism

URL: https://noblefathercreations.com/playbook/ostracism
Also called: Access Removal

You keep being left out of plans, messages and decisions that the rest of the group gets. You cannot point to one moment you could complain about.

Signs it might be this:
- You are the only person missing from messages that everyone else in the circle received.
- The exclusion began or deepened soon after you disagreed, set a limit or raised something awkward.
- When you ask about it, you get vague answers or are told you are overreacting.
- Others are invited while you are out of the room, then mention the event in front of you.
- Information you need to do your role reaches you late or secondhand.

Signs it is probably something else:
- You were told kindly why one event was small, and you were included in the next.
- Several people are out of the loop, you among them.
- When you asked to be added, you were added.
- The gap tracks a clear change such as a new job, a move or different hours.
- The omissions stopped after you reminded people once.
- The group tells you plainly why you were left out of a particular event and includes you in the next one.
- Other members are left out at times too.
- You have stepped back from some things and the invitations have thinned to match.

Sources:
- Williams (2007). Ostracism. Annual Review of Psychology. (Research) https://doi.org/10.1146/annurev.psych.58.110405.085641

## Contribution Erasure

URL: https://noblefathercreations.com/playbook/contribution-erasure
Also called: Curricular Absence, Legacy Erasure, Predecessor Erasure

Contribution Erasure leaves people out of the record. Their presence, contributions or history do not appear in what is taught, shown or remembered.

Signs it might be this:
- The same group or person is left out again and again.
- Requests to include them are met with 'there isn't time' or 'it's not relevant', every time.
- Their contribution was visible before, and later accounts quietly remove it.
- The people left out are often those already less visible.
- You come to wonder whether people like you ever did anything worth recording.

Signs it is probably something else:
- The omission is corrected once raised.
- The record states its scope and points to fuller sources.
- Others are left out for the same practical reasons, without a pattern.
- Credit is being decided fairly, and you disagree with the result.
- The account is new and still being built.
- Omissions are corrected when raised.
- The record is open about its limits.
- There are other places where the missing history or work is fully told.

## Credibility Theft

URL: https://noblefathercreations.com/playbook/credibility-theft
Also called: Competence Undermining, Source Poisoning

Before you say a word, others have been told you exaggerate or get confused. So what you report is doubted before you even speak.

Safety: This often travels with bigger problems. Watch for doubt being planted with people who decide things about you, such as a landlord, employer, family court or doctor. Watch, too, for remarks about your mental state used to explain away a report of harm. Keep dated copies somewhere only you can reach, and speak to a legal aid service or an advocate before the next formal step.

Signs it might be this:
- People you have not yet told anything already seem to hold a version of you.
- The doubt names no particular claim and has no example attached.
- Something you reported gets a reply about your state of mind and not about what you reported.
- The remarks about you come from one source and travel along the same line of people.
- The doubts are raised mostly around times you are about to speak, complain or ask for help.

Signs it is probably something else:
- The doubt is tied to a specific, checkable mistake, which the speaker also names to you.
- The same people trust you on other matters and have been told nothing about you.
- Your account is checked against records and holds up, with no change in how you are treated.
- The person who raised concerns about your reliability said it to you first.
- Skepticism is applied equally to everyone's reports, including the speaker's own.
- The doubt is limited to one claim and is settled by looking at the evidence.
- Every account gets checked, whoever gives it.
- You can learn what has been said about you, and you are given the chance to respond.

Sources:
- Fricker (2007). Epistemic Injustice Power and the Ethics of Knowing. Oxford University PressOxford. (Research) https://doi.org/10.1093/acprof:oso/9780198237907.001.0001

## Priming / Narrative Seeding

URL: https://noblefathercreations.com/playbook/priming-narrative-seeding
Also called: Institutional Contamination, Narrative Injection, Narrative Seeding, Priming

Someone tells you what to think about a person or event before you have seen it yourself. Then what you see seems to prove it.

Signs it might be this:
- The comment arrives just before an encounter, instead of when something relevant came up.
- It tells you how to interpret behavior ('watch how she reacts') rather than describing something that happened.
- Afterward you notice exactly the behavior you were told to expect, and little else.
- The same advance word is given to several people who will all be in the room.
- Asked what the comment was based on, the speaker has no specific event to point to.

Signs it is probably something else:
- The speaker can describe a specific event, with a date, and you can check it yourself.
- They tell you in the same breath what the other person does well.
- They say 'ignore me if it turns out differently' and then actually let it.
- You had formed the same impression on your own before hearing anything.
- The remark gives practical information about the setting, such as parking, deadlines or who has authority to decide.
- The advance word named something specific and checkable, and you checked it.
- The speaker also offered the other side, or said they might be wrong.
- You went in curious, and your impression changed once you met the person.

## Identity-Based Isolation

URL: https://noblefathercreations.com/playbook/identity-based-isolation
Also called: Language Barriers as Isolation

Identity-Based Isolation uses a part of who someone is, often a part that already places them outside the majority, as the reason to quiet them. A concern raised by someone from a minority group is called 'making it about race' or 'divisive'.

Safety: If anyone threatens your immigration status, holds your passport or documents, controls your money or movement, or keeps you from contact with others, this may be a form of serious control or exploitation. Do not confront the person. Contact emergency services if you are in danger, and a specialist support service or qualified immigration or legal adviser in confidence. You can ask whether help is available in your language.

Signs it might be this:
- Your concern is dismissed because of who you are, before anyone looks at what happened.
- You are told, or it is hinted, that speaking up will cause trouble for you because of your identity or status.
- Information or processes are only available in a language you cannot fully use, and requests for help with that are ignored.
- Others in your group are also told their concerns are divisive or personal.
- You are welcome as a face in a photo but not as a voice in a meeting.

Signs it is probably something else:
- Your concern is investigated fully, and the result is explained to you.
- Language support is offered and provided.
- People ask about your experience and take it seriously.
- Disagreement focuses on facts, not on who you are.
- Others from your group are heard and acted upon.
- Concerns are investigated regardless of who raises them.
- Language and access support are provided without fuss.
- People from your group can and do speak up safely.

## Social Mapping

URL: https://noblefathercreations.com/playbook/social-mapping

Social Mapping is the work of learning who matters in a person's life, and then handling each of those people in a planned way. It starts with close interest in someone's friends, family, colleagues and confidants: who they trust, who they listen to, who might notice a change.

Safety: If this pattern comes with control, monitoring, threats, jealousy or fear, it may be part of a wider pattern of coercive control or stalking. Do not confront the person. Contact a specialist domestic abuse or stalking support service or a crisis line, and contact emergency services if you are in danger. Where a child is being targeted by an adult this way, contact child protection services or the police.

Signs it might be this:
- The questions focus on influence: who you listen to, who could change your mind, who would worry.
- Afterwards, the person contacts members of your circle without you, one by one.
- Different people around you seem to have been told different things.
- The people most likely to support you are the ones who drift away first.
- You notice the person treats each of your relationships very differently and cannot explain why.

Signs it is probably something else:
- The person meets your friends and family openly, with you present.
- Your relationships stay as they were, or grow stronger.
- Their questions were about getting to know you, and nothing followed from them.
- They respect your wish to keep some relationships separate.
- The changes in your circle have other clear causes, such as a move or a falling-out.
- The person's contact with your circle is open and includes you.
- Your relationships remain stable or improve.
- They accept it when you keep some relationships to yourself.

## Support System Exhaustion

URL: https://noblefathercreations.com/playbook/support-system-exhaustion
Also called: Victim Redirection

Support System Exhaustion happens when a person seeking help is sent again and again to the same resources, or around the same loop of resources, until they run out of energy and stop asking. 'Have you tried the helpline?' 'Talk to your counselor.' 'Speak to your friends about it.' Each referral sounds supportive. Taken together, they keep the person moving without anything changing, and the people they keep being sent to may also wear out.

Safety: If you are worn out and feeling hopeless, or thinking of harming yourself, contact a crisis line or emergency services now. You do not have to wait for the right referral. If the problem involves abuse, a child's safety, health or immediate danger, contact emergency services or the relevant specialist service directly, and ask someone you trust to help you make contact.

Signs it might be this:
- You have been sent to the same place several times and nothing has changed.
- Different offices or people send you back to each other.
- The person you asked never takes any action themselves.
- The resources you are sent to are already stretched or have told you they cannot help.
- When you stop asking, nobody follows up.

Signs it is probably something else:
- The referral leads to someone who can act, and they do.
- The person referring you checks back to see whether it helped.
- You are offered different options when the first one does not work.
- The service is the right one, and the problem is simply taking time.
- You chose to return to the same support because it helps.
- Referrals lead to action and are followed up.
- You are given new options when old ones fail.
- Someone takes ownership of making sure you get help.

## Pile-Ons / Brigading

URL: https://noblefathercreations.com/playbook/pile-ons-brigading
Also called: Brigading, Pile-Ons, Audience Activation, Pressure Accumulation, dogpiling

Lots of people criticize you at the same moment. Even small comments add up to something you cannot answer or escape.

Signs it might be this:
- Replies arrive in a burst over minutes or hours rather than trickling in over days.
- Many responders react to a quoted piece or screenshot, not the full original.
- The wording of the criticism converges, with the same phrase or insult repeated.
- Responses are about you as a person more than about the specific statement.
- Accounts with no earlier contact with you join, often right after a larger account shares the post.

Signs it is probably something else:
- The responses disagree with one another and include people who defend you.
- Most people quote what you actually said and respond to its content.
- The criticism comes from people you know, raised in separate, calm conversations.
- The volume is small and spread over weeks.
- Someone from the group offers to talk it through, and then does.
- The replies disagree with each other and some defend you.
- It fades within a day or two without new fuel.
- At least one criticism is accurate and you can answer it directly.

## Mobbing

URL: https://noblefathercreations.com/playbook/mobbing

A group keeps picking on one person over weeks or months. Every attempt to raise it gets treated as more proof that the person is the problem.

Signs it might be this:
- The same small group appears across many different incidents over months.
- Complaints about you are vague and secondhand, with no dates, examples or names.
- When you raise one concern, it is answered with a new complaint.
- Colleagues are friendly one-on-one but cold in groups, or say privately that they cannot be seen backing you.
- Your work is checked or measured more closely than that of others in the same role.

Signs it is probably something else:
- Each complaint is specific, dated and describes something you recognize doing.
- The people involved do not know one another or have no contact.
- Feedback is offered to your face with a chance to respond and improve.
- It was a few weeks around a crisis and has eased.
- Others in the same role get similar scrutiny.
- Concerns are put to you directly, with specifics and a chance to answer.
- The people involved change over time and the tension fades.
- A neutral party who reviewed the situation found separate causes for each incident.

Sources:
- Leymann (1990). Mobbing and Psychological Terror at Workplaces. Violence and Victims. (Research) https://doi.org/10.1891/0886-6708.5.2.119

## Scapegoating

URL: https://noblefathercreations.com/playbook/scapegoating
Also called: Sacrificial Repositioning

When something goes wrong for a whole group, one person is named as the cause and punished, and the real problem stays untouched.

Signs it might be this:
- The person blamed had little authority over the decision that failed.
- The group's own role, or its leaders' decisions, are missing from the account.
- Blame is assigned before facts are gathered, or the facts change to fit it.
- The problem comes back after the person is gone.
- The same person tends to be blamed for failures of different kinds.

Signs it is probably something else:
- The review looked at decisions at every level and still found this person's error the main cause.
- The person had the authority and the information to make the call.
- The process was fixed as well as the person dealt with.
- Others who were involved also face consequences.
- The person agrees with the account of what they did.
- The investigation reviewed several levels and the person had a chance to respond.
- Consequences match the person's role and the degree of fault.

## Labeling as Identity Warfare

URL: https://noblefathercreations.com/playbook/labeling-as-identity-warfare
Also called: Condition-Identity Fusion, Deficit Framing, Institutional Language Framing, Labeling, Name Erosion, Program Naming, Strength Invisibility

Someone gets a one-line description like 'the difficult one'. From then on, everything they do, good or bad, is taken as proof of it.

Signs it might be this:
- The same one-line description comes back from people who never saw you in the situation it describes.
- Good behavior gets a footnote ('she's being nice today') instead of counting.
- Your explanation is answered with the label rather than with a reply to what you said.
- The label has been put in writing, in a file, an email thread or a group chat.
- You have become over-careful to avoid fitting it, and the carefulness is read as more evidence.

Signs it is probably something else:
- The description names a specific behavior and a date, and would fall away if the behavior did.
- The person using it can also tell you about times you went against it.
- Several people who never talk to each other describe the same behavior in similar terms.
- The label began as your own joke about yourself and you still like it.
- When you disagree with the description, they listen and adjust the way they talk about you.
- The label is tied to named behaviors and is dropped when the behavior changes.
- It exists only in conversation, not in files or introductions.

## Golden Child Elevation

URL: https://noblefathercreations.com/playbook/golden-child-elevation

One person is held up as the example. Everyone else is regularly measured against them and found lacking.

Signs it might be this:
- The comparison turns up in unrelated conversations, even when the favored person's work has nothing to do with the topic.
- Excuses made for one person are not made for the others for the same behavior.
- Your wins get a brief nod, then a mention of what the favored person did.
- Other relatives repeat the same comparisons, as if it were family policy.
- You have been measured against the same person for years, across more than one age or phase.

Signs it is probably something else:
- Comparisons are rare and tied to one concrete skill.
- Everyone's accomplishments get noticed in a way that feels balanced.
- The comparisons stopped after you mentioned them.
- Differences in treatment follow real differences in need, and have been explained to you.
- The favored person pushes back on the comparisons too.
- Comparisons are occasional and attached to specific accomplishments.
- The family can laugh about it and adjust once someone says it hurts.
- Everyone gets attention for their own strengths over time.

## False Consensus / Social Proof Pressure

URL: https://noblefathercreations.com/playbook/false-consensus-social-proof-pressure
Also called: False Consensus, Normative Messaging, Social Proof Pressure, Early Endorsement Seeding, Gaslighting by Consensus, Petition Legitimation, Phantom Endorsement, Phantom Lead, Pluralistic Ignorance Installation, Social Pressure Layering, Social Proof, Social Proof Amplification, Social Proof Engineering, bandwagon effect

You are told everyone else already agrees, so your doubts seem odd. But nobody can say who 'everyone' is, or they agree less than claimed.

Signs it might be this:
- The group is cited just before you are asked to agree, and not otherwise.
- When you ask 'who?', the answer is vague or turns into annoyance.
- The people named, when you ask them, hold milder or different views.
- The consensus happens to match exactly what the speaker wanted.
- Your disagreement is treated as the issue, with comments about your attitude and not your reasons.

Signs it is probably something else:
- Named people confirm the position when you ask them.
- The speaker invites you to talk to the others and say what you think.
- The decision rests on stated reasons, with the head-count as a side point.
- You are free to hold out, and the group carries on without hostility.
- The count is shown openly, such as a vote or signed list, and you can read it.
- The people mentioned can be asked, and they confirm.
- Disagreement is welcomed, and you can say no without a change in how you are treated.
- The group's view is one point among reasons, not the whole argument.

Sources:
- Ross et al. (1977). The “false consensus effect”: An egocentric bias in social perception and attribution processes. Journal of Experimental Social Psychology. (Research) https://doi.org/10.1016/0022-1031(77)90049-X

## Divide and Conquer

URL: https://noblefathercreations.com/playbook/divide-and-conquer
Also called: Wedge Issue Exploitation, Ally Poisoning, Defensive Withdrawal Induction, Manufactured Conflict, Momentum Collapse, Reentry Disruption

People who would normally compare notes and back each other up drift apart. Each one holds a different version of what the others said.

Signs it might be this:
- Each person has heard something about the other that the other swears they never said.
- Several people are told they are the only ones trusted with certain information.
- Attempts to talk to each other are discouraged, or one person stays the only channel.
- The conflict eases or vanishes once the people involved compare notes directly.
- Alliances between two people tend to cool soon after they form.

Signs it is probably something else:
- When you compare accounts, the stories match.
- Information about everyone is shared freely, in groups.
- The person relaying information stops once corrected.
- The two people have had a conflict of their own for some time.
- The distance followed life changes, such as a move or a new job.
- The go-between welcomes a three-way conversation when asked.
- The distance between the people predates the go-between's involvement.

## Punishment by Proxy

URL: https://noblefathercreations.com/playbook/punishment-by-proxy

After you stand your ground, someone close to you suddenly has a hard time. It is hard to tell whether the two things are connected.

Safety: This tactic can sit beside stalking, threats toward children, pets and relatives, or coercive control, an ongoing pattern of intimidation and rules that limits your life. Warning signs are harm to the third person that follows your refusals, and remarks linking it to you. Another sign is fear of what a disagreement might cost them. Do not confront the person or announce changes. Talk to a domestic violence advocate or legal aid service about a plan for you and the third person. Keep dated notes where the other person cannot see them.

Signs it might be this:
- More than two episodes of third-person trouble follow your disagreements with similar timing.
- The trouble comes from the same person or their circle, not from random sources.
- The third person has no independent history of difficulty with them.
- Remarks link the third person's trouble to what you did, even lightly or as a joke.
- You catch yourself staying quiet to protect someone else.

Signs it is probably something else:
- The third person's difficulty began before your disagreement.
- There is a plain explanation, such as a layoff list or a family illness.
- It happened once and has not repeated after later disputes.
- The third person says their problem with the other person has its own long history.
- The person involved is actively helping the third person.
- A neutral explanation for the third person's trouble exists and can be verified.

## Stochastic Harassment Direction

URL: https://noblefathercreations.com/playbook/stochastic-harassment-direction

Someone keeps painting one person as a villain to a big audience. They never tell anyone to act, yet strangers start harassing that person.

Safety: Harassment waves can move from messages to threats, doxxing or visits to a home or workplace. Take these signs seriously: your address being shared, threats naming you or your family, or someone appearing in person. Keep dated copies and report each wave to the platform. Take the file to the police or a victim-support service, who can advise on protective orders.

Signs it might be this:
- The same person returns to the same target again and again, each time with sharper language.
- Waves of harassment follow the speaker's posts closely and quote their phrases.
- The speaker names or tags the person's employer, school or home area when it adds nothing to the point being made.
- When harassment starts, the speaker disclaims it but keeps going.
- Personal details that the speaker never posted begin to circulate among the audience.

Signs it is probably something else:
- The speaker explicitly condemns the harassment and removes or edits the post.
- The criticism is about a public act of a public figure, and keeps to that act.
- The backlash began before the speaker said anything, from other sources.
- The speaker has not referred to the person again since the first post.
- The person named is a public official or business criticized for what they did in that role.
- The speaker moves on from the topic, or states plainly that nobody should contact the person.
- The criticism concerns something the person did in public, and names no private details.
- The reaction is limited to ordinary replies and does not reach the person's work or family.

## Interruption Patterns

URL: https://noblefathercreations.com/playbook/interruption-patterns
Also called: manterrupting

In meetings or at the table, the same person keeps getting talked over, so their ideas land in pieces or not at all.

Signs it might be this:
- You can count it: across several meetings, the same one or two people are cut off most often.
- The cut-offs land on certain subjects, such as budget, safety or complaints.
- Other people who begin long points in the same minutes go uninterrupted.
- The interrupted person has started leading with their conclusion in one sentence because they expect to lose the floor.
- Saying "I wasn't done" is met with a joke or with "you're being sensitive".

Signs it is probably something else:
- Everyone present is interrupted at about the same rate, including the person who interrupts most.
- The interrupter backs off and says "go on" as soon as it is pointed out.
- It happens on one tense topic only and not otherwise.
- A neutral note-taker tallying the meeting sees no lopsidedness.
- The person who feels cut off also cuts others off at a similar rate.
- The interrupter notices and corrects, for example by handing the floor back.
- Several people share the experience in roughly equal measure.
- A speaking order or timer exists and everyone accepts it.

## Repetition as Truth

URL: https://noblefathercreations.com/playbook/repetition-as-truth
Also called: Reputation Laundering, illusory truth effect

A claim is said so many times, in the same words, with no new proof. It starts to seem true just because you have heard it so often.

Signs it might be this:
- The words of the claim hardly change from one occasion to the next.
- Asking for the basis of the claim brings only another repetition, or irritation.
- You realize you believe the claim but cannot name a single instance behind it.
- The claim is about you and your character, and is repeated even after you give counter-examples.
- Other people begin repeating it, and when you trace it back it all comes from one source.

Signs it is probably something else:
- Each time it comes up, they add a new example, date or document.
- You can look up the thing being repeated and it holds up.
- They are happy to drop it when you show them evidence that it is wrong.
- The repetition has a clear practical purpose, such as a deadline, a rule or a safety step.
- They say it only once or twice, and not as a way to close a conversation.
- Each repetition brings a new detail, example or source that you can check.
- The claim gets updated or dropped when you give evidence against it.
- The repeated phrase is a harmless family or workplace habit, with nothing riding on it.

Sources:
- Hasher et al. (1977). Frequency and the conference of referential validity. Journal of Verbal Learning and Verbal Behavior. (Research) https://doi.org/10.1016/S0022-5371(77)80012-1

## Gaslighting

URL: https://noblefathercreations.com/playbook/gaslighting

Someone keeps telling you that what you clearly remember didn't happen, until you start wondering whether you can trust your own mind.

Signs it might be this:
- The thing being denied is something you can back up with a message, a receipt, or a witness.
- The denial arrives with a comment about you: your memory, your stability, or your habit of exaggerating.
- It happens when you raise a complaint and almost never when the topic is neutral.
- An offer to look at the evidence together is refused or turned into an argument.
- You have started keeping notes or screenshots, not to use them, but to reassure yourself that you are not wrong.

Signs it is probably something else:
- The topic is something neither of you recorded, and both of you admit you may be mixing it up.
- They suggest looking at the message or asking a third person, and then accept what it shows.
- It happened once, in a stressful week, and has not come back.
- The doubt is about your interpretation of an event, not about whether it took place.
- They correct themselves too, with something like 'I got that wrong earlier'.
- The disagreement is about something genuinely unrecorded, and both of you stay open to being wrong.
- They accept the evidence when it is shown, even grudgingly.
- You feel as confident about your memory around other people as you do around this one.

Sources:
- Sweet (2019). The Sociology of Gaslighting. American Sociological Review. (Research) https://doi.org/10.1177/0003122419874843

## Moving Goalposts

URL: https://noblefathercreations.com/playbook/moving-goalposts
Also called: Milestone Migration, Moving the Goalpost, Standards Shifting

You do what was asked, and then the request changes, again and again. You can never reach the point of being done or good enough.

Signs it might be this:
- Each time you finish what was asked, a new and different requirement is named.
- The goal was never put in writing, and the person disputes what was agreed once you meet it.
- The standard has moved several times and always in the direction of more.
- Nobody can say what 'finished' would look like, even when you ask.
- Others doing the same task are told they are fine, while you are not.

Signs it is probably something else:
- The bar changed because of a new fact, and the person said so plainly at the time.
- There is a written spec or rubric, and you are being held to it.
- They can describe what 'done' looks like and sign off when you reach it.
- The extra work is a separate, new request that is offered, not demanded.
- You are the one adding conditions to your own goal.
- The new requirement comes with a reason and is treated as a new task.
- You can ask 'what would make this complete?' and get a straight answer.
- The standard stays put once it is agreed and written.

## Double Binds

URL: https://noblefathercreations.com/playbook/double-binds
Also called: Contradictory Expectations, Double Bind Installation, Paradoxical Injunctions

Whatever you do is wrong. If you do one thing you are criticized for it, and if you do the opposite you are criticized for that too.

Signs it might be this:
- The two demands apply to the same moment, and obeying one directly breaks the other.
- You have tried both options and been faulted for each.
- When you name the contradiction, the answer is that you are being difficult.
- The standard seems to move to whatever you did not do this time.
- The consequences of 'failure' are real, such as cold treatment, anger or loss of something you need.

Signs it is probably something else:
- One of the options is sometimes accepted as the right one.
- The two instructions concern different settings, such as home and work, or different tasks.
- They say 'you're right, I was asking for two things' and adjust.
- The conflict is in the circumstances, such as a tight deadline, not in what they ask of you.
- A third person looking at the demands would see room to meet both.
- The conflicting asks can be talked through, and one of them gives way.
- You are able to satisfy at least one of them at least some of the time.
- They accept being told the messages clash.

Sources:
- Bateson et al. (1956). Toward a theory of schizophrenia. Behavioral Science. (Where the name comes from) https://doi.org/10.1002/bs.3830010402

## Contradiction Stacking

URL: https://noblefathercreations.com/playbook/contradiction-stacking
Also called: Reality Layering

Whatever you say back seems to prove the other half right: first the thing never happened, then it was deserved anyway.

Signs it might be this:
- The denial and the justification both concern the exact same moment, and both are kept alive after you point that out.
- Each new piece of evidence brings a different reason, but never an acknowledgment of the first answer.
- You notice you are arguing against two opposing claims in a single reply.
- The same two-part reply shows up around several unrelated complaints over time.
- You leave the talk unable to say what the other person actually concluded happened.

Signs it is probably something else:
- They say 'I may be wrong about that' and pick one position to stand behind.
- The justification only appears after they have accepted that the event occurred.
- The two statements concern different incidents once you lay them side by side.
- They notice the mismatch themselves and say it sounds contradictory.
- The mixed answers came in one tense moment and have not reappeared.
- One of the two positions is dropped once the mismatch is pointed out.

## Countering

URL: https://noblefathercreations.com/playbook/countering
Also called: Denial, Selective Memory

You say what happened, and you get an instant, sure 'no, it didn't', every time. You never reach the real issue, because you are stuck arguing facts.

Signs it might be this:
- Your account is contradicted in the first sentence of the reply, before any question about details.
- The denial stays in place after you show a message or name someone who was there.
- It happens on many topics, beyond the one where you disagree about what was said.
- You have started opening conversations with proof in hand because you expect to be overruled.
- Your careful wording is itself called 'twisting', so describing events becomes risky.

Signs it is probably something else:
- They say 'let me check' and come back with a correction to their own memory.
- The disagreement is about a thing neither of you wrote down, and both of you say you could be wrong.
- They contradict you on a point of fact but stay curious about why you remember it differently.
- It happens in one heated argument and not in calmer talks.
- They accept the evidence the moment it is shown, even if they are annoyed.
- They contradict you as bluntly as they contradict everyone else, and drop it when shown wrong.
- The disputed point is trivial and you can both laugh about it afterward.
- You still feel free to say 'I remember it differently' and be heard.

## Normalization / Overton Window Manipulation

URL: https://noblefathercreations.com/playbook/normalization-overton-window-manipulation
Also called: Overton Window Manipulation, Normalization, Cycle Perpetuation, Gap Normalization, Institutional Dependency Normalization, Window Shifting

When you say something hurt, you are told it is normal and everyone goes through it. It starts to feel like you are wrong to mind.

Signs it might be this:
- The comparison is used when you describe being hurt, not in other conversations.
- 'Everyone' is never named, and you cannot find a single person who agrees when you ask.
- After the comparison, the person asks you to stop talking about it.
- Your feeling of unease remains while you are being told it is nothing.
- The behavior itself is never discussed, only whether people in general put up with it.

Signs it is probably something else:
- They offer a comparison and then ask what you want to change.
- Someone you trust who knows your situation says it sounds common and still takes the hurt seriously.
- The treatment stops or changes after it is raised.
- The thing is a standard feature of a role that you accepted with open eyes.
- They agree that it is common but not good, and that it can still be addressed.
- The comparison is accurate, checkable and offered with real interest in how you are.
- The behavior stops or softens once you say it hurts.
- You feel free to disagree that it is normal without penalty.

## Thought-Stopping Clichés

URL: https://noblefathercreations.com/playbook/thought-stopping-clich-s
Also called: "That's Just How It Is", thought-terminating cliché

Each time you raise a worry, you get a stock saying like 'don't overthink it'. It ends the topic without answering what you asked.

Signs it might be this:
- The same phrase turns up every time you bring up one particular issue.
- After the phrase, the topic is closed and cannot be returned to.
- Your attempt to say more is met with a further saying, not an answer.
- You are made to feel foolish, ungrateful or negative for asking.
- The phrase answers a practical question, such as who will pay, with a platitude.

Signs it is probably something else:
- They use the phrase and then ask how you are really doing.
- A time to talk is named, such as 'not now, but this weekend', and kept.
- The phrase is offered about something that cannot be fixed, and they remain with you in it.
- They stop saying it when you say it does not help.
- Everyone around you talks in sayings, and they apply to every topic equally.
- The phrase is followed by a question or an offer to talk later.
- They change what they say once you tell them it is not helping.
- It is used about things that cannot be changed, not about things you are asking them to do.

Sources:
- Robert Jay Lifton (1961). Thought Reform and the Psychology of Totalism. (Where the name comes from) https://openlibrary.org/works/OL15241904W

## Word Salad

URL: https://noblefathercreations.com/playbook/word-salad

You ask a simple question and get a long, winding reply that never answers it. Asking again makes it more confusing, and you walk away not knowing what was said.

Signs it might be this:
- The fog arrives on questions where a clear answer would commit them to something.
- The same person is clear and direct on topics that do not involve accountability.
- A request to simplify produces more complexity, not less.
- You come out of the conversation unsure what you asked, as well as what they said.
- Direct, closed questions such as 'yes or no?' are met with another loop.

Signs it is probably something else:
- A simpler, slower question gets a clear answer.
- They speak this way about everything, including topics that are neutral or happy.
- They ask for time to think, and come back with a plain answer.
- There is a known health, language or neurological reason for their speech.
- They say 'I'm not making sense, let me try again', and do.
- They get clearer when the question is made smaller or you give them time.
- The long-winded style shows up with everyone, on every topic.
- They notice and name the muddle themselves and try again.

## Pseudo-Logic

URL: https://noblefathercreations.com/playbook/pseudo-logic
Also called: Circular Arguments, Circular Logic

Every reason you get is just the first claim in new words. The talk goes in circles and never reaches anything you can check.

Signs it might be this:
- You ask 'why do you think that?' and the answer is the claim again, slightly rearranged.
- The reason offered is that the speaker is certain, experienced, or more thoughtful than you.
- Your disagreement is treated as proof of your lack of understanding.
- The talk keeps returning to the same sentence, with no new fact appearing for many minutes.
- A request for a source, example or witness is brushed off as insulting.

Signs it is probably something else:
- A short, independent reason appears when you ask, even if you do not find it convincing.
- They say 'we may just see this differently' and leave the point there.
- The restating is a clarification, and they invite you to say which part is unclear.
- They point to a document, policy or person that you can go and check.
- The loop ends once someone takes a break or sleeps on it.
- An outside fact eventually enters the discussion, even if it arrives late.
- The other person is willing to say what would count as evidence against their claim.
- The loop is limited to one heated topic and does not shape the rest of your talks.

## Ambiguity as Weapon / Strategic Ambiguity

URL: https://noblefathercreations.com/playbook/ambiguity-as-weapon-strategic-ambiguity
Also called: Ambiguity as Weapon, Strategic Ambiguity, Community Confusion Exploitation, Confidentiality Uncertainty

Someone's words can be read two ways. Later you cannot prove what was promised or whether you were being left out, and you are the one left unsure.

Signs it might be this:
- Precise wording appears for the speaker's own tasks and loose wording for what they owe you.
- You ask a direct question and get a smoother, vaguer answer instead of a clearer one.
- After a dispute, the speaker explains what they 'really' meant, and it differs from what the words allowed.
- Different people report hearing different things about the same plan.
- You cannot tell whether you are being excluded, and each time you try to check, the evidence slips away.

Signs it is probably something else:
- Asked to name a date or an amount, they do so without fuss.
- The vagueness spreads across all topics, including ones that cost them something.
- The loose reading goes against them as often as in their favor.
- They tell you at the outset that they do not know yet, and say when they will.
- Others in the same group got the same loose wording, and nobody had firmer information.
- A request for specifics is met with specifics, or an honest 'I don't know yet'.
- The looseness cuts both ways, and the speaker accepts the reading that costs them.
- Others in the same position report the same uncertainty.

Sources:
- Eisenberg (1984). Ambiguity as strategy in organizational communication. Communication Monographs. (Where the name comes from) https://doi.org/10.1080/03637758409390197

## Revisionist History

URL: https://noblefathercreations.com/playbook/revisionist-history
Also called: Memory Manipulation, Narrative Editing, Record Inversion, Retconning, Retroactive Recharacterization

The story of the past gets rewritten to fit the present. Your memory, and often the paperwork, says otherwise, yet you seem out of step.

Signs it might be this:
- A past agreement is described in a way that clearly contradicts what was written or witnessed at the time.
- The retelling changes when the original becomes inconvenient, and holds firm after evidence appears.
- The new version always turns out to favor the teller, in several unrelated stories.
- People who were there say they remember it as you do, and they are called biased or confused.
- You are told 'we've always done it this way' about something that began recently.

Signs it is probably something else:
- The record is thin, and neither person can prove their version.
- They change their account when shown a message and thank you for the correction.
- The retelling changed over years, and no decision or money depends on it.
- They say 'I may be remembering this wrong' before you do.
- Both versions have been shifting, including yours.
- The retelling shifts a little, but they accept the record when it is produced.
- No decision, money or blame depends on which version is true.
- They tell the story differently to different people in a way that is plainly just storytelling.

## Aftercare Control

URL: https://noblefathercreations.com/playbook/aftercare-control

Something hurt you. Afterward you are told it was really for your benefit and you should be grateful, until you question whether it was harmful at all.

Signs it might be this:
- Any mention of the hurt is answered with a reminder of what you supposedly gained.
- You are expected to say thank you for something that frightened or humiliated you.
- The reasons given for the act change over time, but the conclusion that it was kindness never does.
- Your account of how it felt is called dramatic, ungrateful or spoiled.
- You catch yourself telling other people it was good for you, while part of you is unsure.

Signs it is probably something else:
- They accept that it hurt, even while still believing the decision was right.
- You asked why it was done, and the answer comes plainly, without being turned back on you.
- Nobody asks you to be thankful; the explanation is simply offered for you to take or leave.
- The reframe came from you, after your own reflection, and not from the person who made the decision.
- The same person has apologized for other things that went wrong, and changed what they did afterward.
- The person gives a reason and acknowledges the pain in the same breath.
- The subject closes once you have each said your piece, and is not raised again as a debt.
- You can remember it as unfair and still be treated warmly.

## Narrative Monopoly

URL: https://noblefathercreations.com/playbook/narrative-monopoly
Also called: Narrative Capture

Narrative Monopoly, also called Narrative Capture, is control of the dominant story about a situation so that other accounts cannot take hold. One person, group or institution sets the version of events that most people hear, often early and with confidence, and different experiences are treated as exceptions, misunderstandings or complaints from difficult people.

Safety: If the dominant story is covering harm to a child, abuse or a risk to someone's safety, do not rely on internal channels alone. Contact emergency services in immediate danger, or a child protection or specialist support service. If the story is being used in legal or custody matters, get qualified legal advice. Keep your own records.

Signs it might be this:
- Your experience does not match the official or family version, and when you say so you are dismissed.
- Others privately share experiences like yours but say there is no point raising them.
- The same people always get to explain what happened, and others are not asked.
- Questioning the story is treated as an attack on the group or person.
- Information that contradicts the story is left out of meetings, records or announcements.

Signs it is probably something else:
- You are invited to share your account and it is genuinely considered.
- The dominant story changes when new information appears.
- Different views are presented side by side.
- The story reflects most people's experience and differences are acknowledged.
- There are open channels for feedback that lead to visible changes.
- Leaders say plainly where the story might be incomplete.
- Different accounts are recorded, even if not all are agreed with.

## Loaded Language

URL: https://noblefathercreations.com/playbook/loaded-language

A heavy label gets stuck on something ordinary. You end up fighting the word instead of talking about what happened.

Signs it might be this:
- A severe label arrives before anyone has described what happened.
- The same action gets a gentle word for one person and a harsh word for another.
- When you object to the word, the objection is used to show the word was accurate, as in 'only a guilty person would argue.'
- The labels name who you are, and not what you did.
- You catch yourself using their harsh vocabulary about your own behavior.

Signs it is probably something else:
- They are willing to swap the word for a plain description when you ask what they mean.
- The strong word is applied to an act that fits it and backed by specific examples.
- The same vocabulary is used for their own conduct as readily as for yours.
- Their language is dramatic about everything, including small things that do not involve you.
- They take back the label later and say it was heat of the moment.
- The person can restate the complaint in neutral words without losing the point.
- Heavy words appear only in rare, intense moments and are followed by an easier talk afterwards.
- They use the same strong language about their own behavior as about yours.

Sources:
- Robert Jay Lifton (1961). Thought Reform and the Psychology of Totalism. (Where the name comes from) https://openlibrary.org/works/OL15241904W

## Exaggeration

URL: https://noblefathercreations.com/playbook/exaggeration

A specific problem gets turned into 'you never' or 'you always'. Then you end up arguing about the word, not about what happened.

Signs it might be this:
- Asked for an example, the person repeats the absolute more loudly instead of naming a date.
- A counterexample you offer is brushed off as 'that doesn't count'.
- The sweeping word turns up in nearly every complaint, whatever the subject.
- The claim grows between tellings: 'a few times' on Monday, 'always' by Friday.
- The conversation ends up about whether 'never' is accurate, and the original request is never answered.

Signs it is probably something else:
- When asked for an example, they give one and the claim shrinks to fit: 'Okay, not always, but the last three times.'
- The big word is followed by a specific request you can act on.
- They use absolutes about themselves too, as in 'I always mess this up'.
- You can count, and it really is nearly every time.
- They laugh or soften when you point out it isn't literally true.
- A specific example arrives as soon as you ask for one.
- Big words are simply how this person talks in every mood and about every topic.

## Forged Screenshots / Edited Evidence

URL: https://noblefathercreations.com/playbook/forged-screenshots-edited-evidence
Also called: Forged Screenshots, Deepfakes, Edited Recordings, Fabricated Evidence, Deepfake Video/Audio

Someone shows others a screenshot or document that looks real but was made up or changed. They present it as proof of something you never wrote, said or did.

Safety: A fabricated record may be used in a custody dispute, a protective-order hearing, a workplace complaint or a threat of exposure. It can cost you housing, income, children or safety, so treat it as a legal matter and not as an argument. Save originals with their dates, delete nothing, and speak to a lawyer or legal aid before replying to the person who produced it. If you fear for your safety, an advocate can help you plan.

Signs it might be this:
- The record contradicts your own copy of the same conversation in wording, order or dates.
- The phrasing is unlike your own, or it mentions events you never took part in.
- Only an image is offered, never the original device, account export or file.
- Neither the platform nor anyone else can match the item to a real message.
- The item appears just as a decision is being made about you, such as a hearing, review or breakup.

Signs it is probably something else:
- Your own copy of the thread, once you look, matches it.
- The difference is a cropped section or a missing earlier message, not changed words.
- The platform's own export confirms the messages and dates.
- The person who sent it also shares the original and invites you to compare.
- The odd formatting is explained by a different phone, language setting or app version.
- The original can be opened and checked, and it matches what you were shown.
- The person corrects the record when shown your copy.
- The disagreement is about what a real message meant, not whether it was written.

## Lying by Omission / Gaslighting by Omission

URL: https://noblefathercreations.com/playbook/lying-by-omission-gaslighting-by-omission
Also called: Gaslighting by Omission, Selective Information Sharing, Strategic Incompleteness, Lying by Omission, Information Drip

You are told true things, but not the one fact that would have changed what you decided. You find out later, from someone else or by accident, that it was known all along.

Signs it might be this:
- The missing detail is exactly the one that would have changed your decision.
- The person knew the fact at the time, and a record or a third party shows it.
- Direct questions on the topic get answers that are accurate but still go around it.
- Earlier accounts from them have a similar shape: the favorable parts in, the complicating ones out.
- When the fact comes out, the first response defends the omission ('you didn't ask') rather than addressing the fact.

Signs it is probably something else:
- They tell you the missing piece as soon as they realize it matters.
- They did not know it themselves until recently.
- The omitted matter is truly theirs, or a third party's, to keep private, and does not affect your decision.
- They volunteered a bigger and uncomfortable fact just before, which does not fit a filter.
- When asked directly, they answer directly.
- The missing piece was small and had no bearing on any choice you made.
- It happened during a hectic period and has not repeated.

## Vague Allegations with High Consequences

URL: https://noblefathercreations.com/playbook/vague-allegations-with-high-consequences
Also called: Vague Allegations

Someone says there are complaints about you but won't say who, what or when. You can't answer them, so you are left to imagine the worst.

Signs it might be this:
- Asking 'who?' or 'what did they say?' gets 'I can't say' every time, and the claim still stands.
- The statement is presented as settled fact: 'everyone knows'.
- The remark arrives soon after you disagree, ask for something or raise a complaint.
- You are told to change but not told what to change.
- The details shift or vanish when you probe.

Signs it is probably something else:
- When you ask what behavior is meant, they describe one, even if they won't say who raised it.
- They say plainly it is only their impression and invite your side.
- The concern is formally recorded and you are given a process to respond.
- They come back later with specifics.
- It was said once, and they looked surprised to be pressed.
- A reason for the vagueness is given and the behavior is described.
- The speaker offers to find out more and returns with an answer.
- You are invited to give your own account.

## Compartmentalization

URL: https://noblefathercreations.com/playbook/compartmentalization
Also called: Confidential Disclosure Seeding, Selective Information Sharing

Everyone in the family or team is told a different piece. No one can see the whole story or notice that something doesn't add up.

Signs it might be this:
- When two people compare what they were told, the accounts differ in ways that matter.
- The same person is the only route between the groups.
- Requests for secrecy are steady and sit around the matters that would draw questions.
- Asking 'who else knows?' gets evasion.
- Someone who asked across groups was told to leave it.

Signs it is probably something else:
- The reason for separation is stated and fits, such as the privacy of a medical matter or a client.
- The person encourages you to share and compare what you know.
- Information flows when you ask for it.
- The separation follows role, like payroll versus marketing, and applies equally to everyone.
- Nothing important differs between accounts when you compare them.
- A reason is offered and you can check it.
- You are openly encouraged to speak to anyone.

## Half-Truth Framing

URL: https://noblefathercreations.com/playbook/half-truth-framing
Also called: Paltering, Selective Disclosure, Selective Truth Weaponization

Everything said is true, yet you walk away believing something that is not. Each fact checks out, so the problem only shows when you see what was left around it.

Signs it might be this:
- The answer addresses a neighboring question, not the one you asked.
- When the missing context is added, the impression it created falls apart.
- Challenging the impression gets 'but everything I said was true' and no acknowledgment of what you were led to believe.
- It shows up on topics where the full picture would cost the speaker something.
- A plain yes or no was available, and a longer answer was given instead, again and again.

Signs it is probably something else:
- Adding the missing context leaves the picture unchanged.
- They accept 'that's not what I understood' and fill in the rest without being pressed.
- The same wordy, precise style shows up on every topic, including ones with nothing at stake.
- The speaker did not know the full picture themselves.
- You were told the limits at the start: 'I can only speak to this part.'
- The person fills in the missing context as soon as you ask.
- The slanted account came from a hurried summary and not from a conversation about something that mattered.
- The impression was minor, and correcting it costs neither side anything.

## Frame Control / False Framing

URL: https://noblefathercreations.com/playbook/frame-control-false-framing
Also called: False Framing, Frame Assassination, PSYOP Message Framing, Frame Control, Community Reframing, Problem Identification (Selective)

The talk keeps getting turned into a talk about something else, often you. What you actually wanted to say never gets an answer.

Signs it might be this:
- Your complaint names an action and the reply names a trait.
- You can state your point three times and each time end up back at the new topic.
- A label is attached to the situation before anyone has described what happened.
- The conversation ends with you apologizing for how you raised it.
- Days later, the original issue has no answer and nobody has mentioned it.

Signs it is probably something else:
- Your original point gets an answer, even a disagreeing one, before anything else is raised.
- They ask 'can I say how this feels to me first?' and then return to your issue.
- The concern about you is specific, such as that you have been sleeping badly, and they stay on your topic too.
- The strong label still holds when the facts are listed plainly.
- A time to resume is named and kept.
- The subject changes only when both of you are worn out, and returns when you are rested.
- A strong label, once checked against the facts, turns out to hold.

## Burden of Proof Shifting / Sealioning

URL: https://noblefathercreations.com/playbook/burden-of-proof-shifting-sealioning
Also called: Burden of Proof Shifting, Sealioning, shifting the burden of proof

Someone politely asks you to prove and explain, again and again. Nothing you give is ever enough, until you are too tired to keep going.

Signs it might be this:
- You give a source and the reply questions the source, then another source, then a word in it.
- You are asked to explain the basics of a topic after saying you will not debate it.
- The asker never says what they believe or what evidence would satisfy them.
- The polite tone holds while the number of requests grows, and your dropping patience is then pointed out.
- Leaving the thread is met with a claim that you could not answer.

Signs it is probably something else:
- The person quickly states their own position, so you can see what the questions are for.
- They acknowledge a source you give and move on to a new point.
- The questions slow or stop when you say you cannot continue.
- The asker has to act on the answer, like a decision-maker who needs the facts.
- The conversation is one you opened or agreed to, such as a debate or an interview.
- They say what would satisfy them and accept it when it arrives.
- The questions connect to a decision that rests with them.
- They say thanks and drop the subject when you step away.

## Gish Gallop / Firehose of Falsehood

URL: https://noblefathercreations.com/playbook/gish-gallop-firehose-of-falsehood
Also called: AI-Driven Narrative Hijacking, Firehose of Falsehood, Gish Gallop, Memory Flooding, shotgun argumentation

Someone throws out so many points so fast that you cannot answer them all, then treats every unanswered one as a point won.

Signs it might be this:
- You answer one claim thoroughly and the response is a new list rather than a reply to your answer.
- When you check the claims later, many turn out to be wrong or unrelated to the point they were meant to support.
- The pace leaves no room for you to say anything between claims.
- Silence on any point is announced as a win.
- Asking to take one point at a time is met with 'so you can't answer the others'.

Signs it is probably something else:
- They are willing to slow down and take one claim at a time when you ask.
- Most of the individual claims hold up when you check them.
- The claims relate to one main argument rather than scattering over many topics.
- You are in a setting like a briefing, where the speaker is expected to cover a lot of material.
- The other person also gives you room to make your own points at length.
- Most claims survive a close look and the speaker corrects those that do not.
- They agree to deal with the points in an order you can both follow.
- The flood is a one-time burst of excitement rather than their regular way of arguing.

Sources:
- Paul and Matthews (2016). The Russian "Firehose of Falsehood" Propaganda Model: Why It Might Work and Options to Counter It. RAND Corporation. (Research) https://doi.org/10.7249/PE198

## Dog Whistling / Coded Signaling

URL: https://noblefathercreations.com/playbook/dog-whistling-coded-signaling

A comment sounds normal to everyone, but you or a certain group hear a second message. The speaker can always say they meant nothing.

Signs it might be this:
- The same ordinary-sounding phrase keeps coming just before a real consequence for you, such as money, contact or approval being withdrawn.
- Only you and the speaker seem to understand the weight of the phrase.
- It refers to something that was earlier said as a clear threat or warning, and is now said as if casual.
- When you say it bothered you, the answer is 'I didn't say anything wrong', and the phrase is repeated later.
- Several people in a group use the same odd phrase in a way that excludes one person.

Signs it is probably something else:
- The phrase has no consistent link to any consequence for you.
- The speaker explains what they meant and the explanation is consistent over time.
- The reference comes from something you have both laughed about before.
- A trusted third person who knows the context hears nothing in it.
- The only evidence is how the phrase made you feel, with no earlier event to connect it to.
- The speaker is willing to stop using it when you say it bothers you.
- Other people who know the history see an ordinary comment.

## Emotional Sequencing

URL: https://noblefathercreations.com/playbook/emotional-sequencing
Also called: Emotional Non Sequiturs, Erratic Emotional Behavior

Emotional Sequencing is a rapid run of emotions, such as warmth, anger, tears, coldness and cheer, that does not follow from anything that happened. The receiver cannot predict which mood will meet them and spends their energy tracking it.

Safety: Mood swings on their own are not a danger signal, and many have health causes that deserve care rather than blame. It becomes serious if the swings include rage, threats, breaking things, physical harm, or fear for children in the home. In that case, put your own and any children's safety first, call emergency services if you are in immediate danger, and contact a specialist domestic abuse service. If the person talks about harming themselves, contact a crisis line or emergency services.

Signs it might be this:
- The mood shifts often line up with moments when you set limits or raise concerns.
- After a swing, the original issue is never returned to.
- You find yourself apologizing or giving in just to bring back the calm.
- Other people close to the person describe the same sudden switches.
- The person later denies or plays down the shifts.

Signs it is probably something else:
- The person is open about their mood changes and how they manage them.
- The changes happen whatever you say or ask.
- They come back to the issue once calm.
- There is a clear cause, such as bad news, pain or exhaustion.
- The swings are rare and they make repair afterward.
- They name the swings and work on them, perhaps with support.
- Issues are picked up and settled once things are calm.
- You feel free to raise concerns without dreading the next mood.

## Authority Hijack

URL: https://noblefathercreations.com/playbook/authority-hijack
Also called: Credential Asymmetry Deployment

Someone tells you what you really feel or mean, and treats your own explanation of your own mind as the thing that needs fixing.

Signs it might be this:
- Your stated feeling is treated as a mistaken first draft.
- You have said 'that's not what I meant' and been told what you meant anyway.
- The other person's reading is never offered as a question.
- It happens when your feelings are inconvenient for them, such as when you are hurt by something they did.
- You end up arguing about what you feel instead of about what happened.

Signs it is probably something else:
- Their reading is offered as a question and dropped once you answer.
- They say 'I could be wrong' and visibly mean it.
- The reading is about visible behavior and not about your inner state.
- You asked for their view of what you might be feeling.
- The person has nothing riding on what you feel.
- The reading is a question and drops when you decline it.
- It is offered only when you ask for an outside perspective.
- Their interpretation is about your behavior, and your account of your reasons stands.

## False Authority

URL: https://noblefathercreations.com/playbook/false-authority

Someone gives you their opinion but speaks as if it were plain fact. If you disagree, it sounds as though you are the one being irrational.

Signs it might be this:
- Your disagreement is described as emotion or bias, while theirs never is.
- You ask for the source or reasoning and are told it is obvious.
- The same person is 'objective' about topics where they have a clear stake in the outcome.
- You are treated as having a feeling about a thing, while they are treated as having the truth about it.
- Different views are never described as views, only as right and wrong.

Signs it is probably something else:
- They can name where the claim comes from and are glad for you to check it.
- They change their position when you give a good reason.
- The topic really does have a settled factual answer and they are simply reporting it.
- They apply the same standard to their own bias, saying things like 'I'm not neutral on this'.
- The confident tone is how they sound about everything, and they are still open to being questioned.
- They offer their sources, and you are free to weigh them.
- They are as ready to say 'that's my view' as to say 'that's the fact'.
- The claim is within an area where they hold real, checkable expertise.

## Credential-Costuming

URL: https://noblefathercreations.com/playbook/credential-costuming
Also called: false credentials

Someone leans on a title or affiliation that is invented or inflated, and so you stop asking the questions you would normally ask.

Signs it might be this:
- The institution or licensing body has no record of the person, or the credential is missing from a public register.
- The title is used mainly to end questions ('I'm the expert here') and not to support an explanation.
- Basic follow-up questions about the claimed field get vague or inconsistent answers.
- The details of the credential shift between tellings: different years, different schools, different roles.
- The credential is offered in place of evidence precisely when a claim is challenged.

Signs it is probably something else:
- A quick check of the register or the institution confirms the title.
- The person explains the credential's limits unprompted, such as 'my degree is in a related field.'
- They welcome follow-up questions and answer with working knowledge.
- The mismatch is only that you did not recognize the title or the institution.
- The claim is small, easy to confirm, and tied to what they are actually asking you to do.
- The credential checks out when you look it up, and the person's knowledge fits it.
- The claim is minor and has no bearing on money, health or safety decisions.
- They correct any overstatement as soon as you point it out.

## Pseudo-Profundity / Intellectual Intimidation

URL: https://noblefathercreations.com/playbook/pseudo-profundity-intellectual-intimidation
Also called: Complexity-as-Authority

Someone speaks in big, abstract words that sound impressive but never land on anything concrete. You end up feeling too slow to question it.

Signs it might be this:
- When you ask what a term means, the answer uses more terms of the same kind.
- You can nod along to the whole explanation and then find you cannot repeat a single thing it said.
- The explanation ends in a request for you to pay, sign or agree to something you cannot yet restate.
- Your confusion is treated as a sign that you lack the background, rather than as a reason to explain better.
- Other people in the room look equally lost but nobody says so.

Signs it is probably something else:
- They can restate the point in plain words when you ask, and it still holds up.
- They check that you are following and slow down when you are not.
- The vocabulary is standard in their field and they explain the terms unprompted.
- A concrete example or a diagram makes the idea clear.
- They readily say 'I'm not sure' or 'that part is still debated'.
- A plain restatement keeps the meaning and answers your question.
- They are as comfortable saying 'I don't know' as they are with technical terms.
- Your confusion is met with patience, and the terms are defined as they go.

Sources:
- Pennycook et al. (2015). On the reception and detection of pseudo-profound bullshit. Judgment and Decision Making. (Research) https://doi.org/10.1017/S1930297500006999

## Just Asking Questions

URL: https://noblefathercreations.com/playbook/just-asking-questions
Also called: JAQing off

Just Asking Questions puts an accusation or false claim in the form of a question. 'I'm not saying anything, but why did she leave so early?' 'Has anyone checked where the money went?' The claim gets into people's heads, and the speaker can step back by saying they only asked. Questions are how people find out the truth, and most questions are what they seem.

Safety: Insinuating questions are damaging but are not always a safety risk. They become one when they lead to threats, harassment, people turning up at your home, or exposure of private details, or when they put your job, children or legal position at risk. In that case, keep records, report to the platform or organization, and get qualified legal advice. Contact emergency services if you feel in danger.

Signs it might be this:
- The question only makes sense if you already assume the worst.
- There is no evidence behind it, and the speaker does not offer any.
- Answers are ignored, and the question returns in a new form.
- The questions are asked in public, or in a group, rather than to the person.
- When challenged, the speaker says they never claimed anything.

Signs it is probably something else:
- The person asking accepts a clear answer and drops it.
- They bring the question to you directly and privately.
- They have a real reason for asking and say what it is.
- They are as interested in answers that clear you as in ones that don't.
- It was a single clumsy question, not a series.
- Questions are asked in private and answers are accepted.
- The asker explains why they are asking.
- The questions stop once the facts are clear.

## Motte-and-Bailey

URL: https://noblefathercreations.com/playbook/motte-and-bailey
