- You cannot trace who edited or posted the material, and are guessing at motive.
- The error gets corrected quickly once it is reported, with a visible record.
- The claim is easy to cross-check against a primary source you can reach yourself.
- The mistake is minor and affects nothing you are deciding.

## Data Harvesting

URL: https://noblefathercreations.com/playbook/data-harvesting
Also called: Ambient Data Collection, Data Accumulation, Data Point Extraction, Profile Construction

Data Harvesting is the continuous collection of detailed information about someone, such as where they go, what they do, how they feel or how they perform, built into a profile far beyond what the service needs. Apps, devices, platforms, workplaces and schools may gather it in the background.

Safety: If you think a partner, relative or someone close is collecting data about you through your devices or accounts, do not confront them or suddenly remove the tool, as that can raise risk. Contact a domestic abuse helpline or digital-safety specialist first to plan safely. If you are in danger, call emergency services.

Signs it might be this:
- The data collected is far broader than the service needs to work.
- You only learn about the collection by accident or by searching deep in settings.
- Saying no means losing access to something you must use, like a school or work system.
- Data from different parts of your life seems to be joined together.
- You cannot find out how long it is kept or who can see it.

Signs it is probably something else:
- Collection is limited to what the service needs and is clearly explained.
- You can turn off extra collection without losing the main service.
- Data is deleted after a stated time.
- You can see what is held about you on request.
- The worry comes from one setting that was switched on by mistake and is easy to change.
- Collection is limited, explained and easy to control.
- You can see and delete your data.
- The service responds openly to questions about what it gathers.

## Data Onward Sharing

URL: https://noblefathercreations.com/playbook/data-onward-sharing
Also called: De-identification Laundering, Non-Consensual Distribution, Secondary Market Exploitation

Data Onward Sharing is when information collected for one purpose is passed, sold or shown to others without the person's real knowledge. A school survey, a health app, a loyalty card or a work system gathers data for its stated use, and it then travels to partners, vendors, advertisers or researchers.

Safety: If intimate images or private messages have been shared, or sharing is being used to threaten you, it may be a crime. Keep evidence safely and do not engage with the person. Contact the police or a specialist support service. If children's images are involved, report to the police right away. If you feel overwhelmed, a crisis line can help.

Signs it might be this:
- You see ads, contact or decisions that seem to come from information you gave somewhere else.
- The service cannot or will not say who it shares data with.
- Sharing is described only as 'with trusted partners'.
- You never had a real chance to say no to sharing.
- Private images or messages you sent to one person have been seen by others.

Signs it is probably something else:
- You were told plainly, in advance, who would receive the data and why.
- The sharing is needed for the service you asked for.
- You can opt out of extra sharing and still use the service.
- Only broad summaries that cannot identify you are shared.
- The match between your data and an ad was a coincidence and can be explained.
- Sharing is limited, stated plainly and needed for the service.
- You can refuse extra sharing without losing the main service.
- The organization answers questions about who received what.

## Swatting

URL: https://noblefathercreations.com/playbook/swatting

Swatting is when someone makes a false emergency report so that an armed or emergency response arrives at another person's home, school or workplace. It turns the emergency services into a weapon against the target.

Safety: Treat this as an emergency safety risk. If responders arrive, follow their instructions calmly and do not make sudden movements. Never confront the person you think is responsible. Report every incident to the police and ask how your address can be flagged. Save all evidence. If threats continue, contact emergency services right away and seek victim support and legal advice. If the fear becomes overwhelming, a crisis line or a doctor can help.

Signs it might be this:
- Emergency responders arrive describing a situation that is not happening and has no basis at all.
- It came after an online fight, a breakup or threats from someone who knows your address.
- Your address or personal details were posted online shortly before.
- Someone hints afterward that they caused it, or mocks you about it.
- It has happened more than once, or to others in the same online group.

Signs it is probably something else:
- A neighbor explains they heard something that sounded like an emergency.
- A relative or friend says they asked for a welfare check out of real worry.
- An alarm or device triggered the call.
- The call was made to the wrong address by mistake.
- Responders found a real problem you were not aware of.
- There is a clear, honest explanation, such as an alarm or a good-faith caller.
- It happened once and no link to any conflict is found.
- The caller comes forward and explains a genuine mistake.

## Uncorrected Record

URL: https://noblefathercreations.com/playbook/uncorrected-record
Also called: Correction Invisibility, Permanent Digital Residue

Uncorrected Record is when an accusation is made in public, loudly and in a lasting form, while any correction is quiet, private or missing altogether, so the first version is the one people remember. A post naming someone spreads widely, and the later note that they were cleared reaches almost nobody.

Safety: A false claim that stays public is mainly a reputation harm, but it can turn dangerous. If it leads to threats, people turning up at your home, or harassment, put safety first: contact emergency services if you are in danger, save evidence, and use platform reporting tools. If the claim affects your job, schooling, custody or legal position, get qualified legal advice. If it leaves you feeling hopeless, contact a crisis line or a doctor.

Signs it might be this:
- The claim was made before an audience, but the clearing came by private message or a quiet update.
- Asking for a correction to the same audience was refused or ignored.
- The original post or statement is still visible with no note added.
- People still treat you as guilty and say they never heard otherwise.
- Search results or screenshots keep the claim alive, and the source will not add a correction where it would be seen.

Signs it is probably something else:
- A correction was made in the same place and with similar prominence.
- The original claim was removed and replaced with a clear note.
- You asked for wider correction and it was given, even if late.
- The claim was never public, and you are worried about a rumor rather than a record.
- The accusation was later found to be true.
- The source agrees to add a correction where the original appeared.
- The claim has been taken down and the source has said so openly.
- The source helps you reach people who heard the claim.

## Intimate Image Abuse

URL: https://noblefathercreations.com/playbook/intimate-image-abuse
Also called: Deepfake / AI Voice / SIM Swap / Intimate Image Abuse / Smart-Home Coercion, revenge porn, image-based sexual abuse, non-consensual intimate images

Someone shares, or says they will share, private sexual pictures or videos of you without your agreement. The images are sometimes real and sometimes faked.

Safety: Take these seriously: a deadline, a demand that keeps growing, or contact from several accounts. Also take seriously messages to your family or workplace, and threats of self-harm used to keep you quiet. If shame feels unbearable, a crisis line can help tonight. If the person shown is under 18, treat it as urgent and contact your country's child-safety or police service. Save links and screenshots, then ask an advocate about takedown options before replying.

Signs it might be this:
- A specific threat names the images, who would see them and what you must do to stop it.
- Images appear, or are shown to others, that you did not agree to share.
- The threat starts, or returns, after you end contact or begin a new relationship.
- An unknown account contacts you after a private chat and shows part of your image or your contact list.
- A fake explicit image of you circulates, whether or not you ever took a photo.

Signs it is probably something else:
- Nothing has been shared or threatened, and the images were given in a relationship that remains on good terms.
- The message is a vague boast with no mention of images, who would see them or what you must do.
- The only images are ones a couple openly agreed to keep, and both understand what they are for.
- Everyone shown agreed to the use, with no pressure.
- The message went to hundreds of people as a template, and no real image of you was ever included. It is still worth reporting.
- No image exists or has been shown, and the message is generic and sent to many people.
- The images stayed private after an amicable end.
- A copy was removed from the platform where it appeared, and you can see the link no longer works.

Sources:
- McGlynn and Rackley (2017). Image-Based Sexual Abuse. Oxford Journal of Legal Studies. (Research) https://doi.org/10.1093/ojls/gqw033

## Reputation Hijacking

URL: https://noblefathercreations.com/playbook/reputation-hijacking

Reputation Hijacking is when someone else takes control of how you are presented to other people. They speak for you, describe you, post about you or set the story about who you are, so that by the time your own account arrives, people have already formed a view.

Safety: If the person is sharing private images, your address or your location, making threats, or encouraging others to target you, treat it as a safety matter. Keep evidence, report to the platform and, if you feel at risk, contact emergency services or a specialist support service for harassment or abuse. Qualified legal advice can help with serious false statements. Do not confront the person directly if they have been threatening or controlling.

Signs it might be this:
- People treat you differently and later say they 'heard' something about you from one source.
- You are not given a chance to answer what was said, or the space where it was said blocks your reply.
- Someone speaks for you, claiming to know your intentions, plans or feelings.
- Searching your name, or asking mutual contacts, shows a version of you that one person seems to have built.
- The account given of you changes your access to work, school, teams or social groups.

Signs it is probably something else:
- You are told what was said and offered a real chance to respond.
- The comment reflects something you did and can acknowledge, even if it stings.
- Different people formed their views independently, without one source guiding them.
- The person corrects their account when you show them it is inaccurate.
- There is a fair way to add your own statement to a record or answer a post.
- The person changes what they say once they hear your account.
- Most people who know you still form their own view.
